cards.36.who: PM, Eng, HM. Scored on: practical, has clear criteria.
cards.36.why: The "reversible vs irreversible" frame (like Amazon's "one-way / two-way door") is clear and easy to use. The example fits the security industry. "Quality bar per release" is a concrete tool. And it links to AI.

cards.37.who: Vy, HM, HRBP. Source: Qualgo's Coach culture. Scored on: method, results.
cards.37.why: The opening line takes a clear position. The three principles are easy to apply. The numbers are real. It ends with a modest, moving measure of success. It ties straight to Qualgo's "Coach" value.
cards.37.five: One specific mentee story (anonymised) and the measure "they challenge my design with a better argument".

cards.38.who: HM, HRBP, CEO. Source: a standard behavioural question for every lead role; reviews about Qualgo's management culture. Scored on: courage, respect, results.
cards.38.understand: 🟨 **It must be a real story.** Pick one from Hearti Lab (team of 3), Toastmasters (members), or NAB (colleagues or stakeholders). The frame below uses the **SBI** model (Situation, Behaviour, Impact) from the Center for Creative Leadership, a widely recognised frame. Replace the square brackets with the facts.
cards.38.why: It has one imperfect detail (you waited too long). It uses the professional SBI frame. It has one specific spoken line. You find that the problem was in your own system (humble and mature). And it ends with a lesson you can apply.
cards.38.five: A real story, with the detail that you waited too long, the exact SBI line, and the lesson "the gap was in my system".
cards.38.evidence: 🟨 **Illustrative frame. Replace it with a real story before Day 7.**
cards.38.image: Desk 7: **three bricks** stacked up (S, B, I). On top sits a **clock** that is already past time (you waited too long).
cards.38.must: (1) a detail where you didn't do well; (2) a specific SBI line; (3) ask before you conclude; (4) the result; (5) the lesson.
cards.38.drill: Say the SBI line out loud as if you were really talking to that person.
cards.38.follow_ups.1.a: 🟨 a second story (for example with a stakeholder at NAB).
cards.38.traps: A story where you were perfect. No specific spoken line. The other person is the "bad guy".
cards.39.who: Mobile Eng Tuấn, Eng Hải. Scored on: understands what engineers need, doesn't miss states.
cards.39.why: The "hand-over" opening is a position with personality. Your developer background builds instant empathy with engineers. Four concrete parts. A chat example. A link to vibe-coding.
cards.39.five: Bring P5 into the room. Mention your developer background. Review on a real device before shipping.
cards.39.evidence: ✅ 4 years as a developer. ✅ Cursor for the stablecoin wallet. ✅ handover checklist (if the Q39 story is real).
cards.39.image: Desk 8: two hands **passing a box** (hand-over), not throwing it over a wall. The box has 4 compartments.
cards.39.must: (1) engineers from the start; (2) 4 parts; (3) developer background; (4) review on a real device.

cards.39.follow_ups.0.a: **"Yes, plus a short Loom for anything complex."** 🟨 (only name tools you really use)
cards.39.traps: "I give them the Figma link". Not mentioning error states.
cards.40.who: HM, HRBP. Source: the JD (you may build a team); reviews about the 3-hour test. Scored on: clear criteria, fairness.
cards.40.why: It has a clear priority order and a specific technique (the "feedback moment"). It takes a view on fairness. And it raises the 3-hour test issue (from reviews) with tact, as a contribution, not a complaint.
cards.40.five: Three criteria in order, the "feedback moment", and a view on fair process without criticising their test.
cards.40.evidence: ✅ Hired 3 people at Hearti Lab. 🟨 "feedback moment was the best predictor": only say it if it's true. ⚠️ The line about long tests: only say it if the interviewer is open to it; with TA you can drop it.
cards.40.image: Desk 9 (the last one): **a scale with three pans**. One holds a brain, one a pencil, one an ear.
cards.40.must: (1) three criteria in order; (2) feedback moment; (3) fair process; (4) Hearti Lab.
cards.40.drill: Write 3 interview questions you'd ask a designer candidate.

cards.41.who: PM Mai, HM. Source: standard behavioural question; the "Act with transparency" value. Scored on: respect, data, results, solving the problem rather than "winning".
cards.41.understand: Mai is quietly asking: *"Will this person be tiring to work with?"* A good story: you disagreed for the user's sake, used evidence, proposed an experiment, and were **ready to be wrong**. 🟨 Pick a real story (Merchant Services or CIB). Replace the square brackets in the frame below.
cards.41.why: "Opinion against opinion" is what PMs hate. You show that you ask "why", use experiments, accept the PM's goal as valid, and are ready to lose. These are the four signals a PM wants to see.
cards.41.five: A real story with an experiment, respect for the PM's goal, and a story where you lost, ready for when they ask next.
cards.41.evidence: 🟨 **Illustrative frame.** Link it to Merchant (70% faster onboarding) only if the real story comes from that project.
cards.41.image: Pantry, coffee machine: **two cups of coffee** (two options) on **a scale**. You hand your cup to the PM if the other one is heavier.
cards.41.must: (1) ask the PM's goal; (2) a third option; (3) test; (4) ready to lose.
cards.41.drill: Prepare a story where you **lost**, and why that was the right result.
cards.41.traps: A story where you "won" and the PM was wrong. Speaking badly of the PM.
cards.42.who: Eng Hải, Mobile Eng Tuấn. Scored on: respects constraints, creative, understands the tech.
cards.42.why: "First, I believe them" is the line engineers most want to hear. The 80/20 rule is practical. There's a way out when the value really matters. Your developer background sets you apart.
cards.42.five: "First, I believe them" + ask which part is expensive + one real example where you simplified a design yourself while coding the wallet.
cards.42.evidence: ✅ 4 years as a developer. 🟨 one real example (for example on the stablecoin wallet, when you coded it yourself and simplified a design).
cards.42.image: Pantry fridge: a **long receipt** with **only one line marked in yellow** (the expensive part).
cards.42.must: (1) believe them; (2) which part is expensive; (3) the need vs how you drew it; (4) developer background.
cards.42.drill: Think of one real example from the stablecoin wallet.
cards.42.traps: Defending the design at all costs. Giving in at once.
cards.43.who: HM, HRBP, CEO (who may be the one asking). Source: reviews mention a top-down management culture; HiPPO. Scored on: courage, handling politics well, not being stubborn.
cards.43.why: It starts with respect (the CEO may be the one asking). It moves from morals to concrete risk (language a CEO understands). It has an experiment and "disagree and commit". And it has one clear line, framed as a shared value.
cards.43.five: Respect first, concrete risk rather than morals, an experiment, and one line framed as a shared value.
cards.43.evidence: ✅ point of view. 🟨 a real example with a senior leader at NAB or a freelance client.
cards.43.image: Pantry standing desk: **a hippo** (HiPPO) wearing a tie. You hand it **a pair of binoculars** (so it can see).
cards.43.must: (1) respect; (2) concrete risk, not empty morals; (3) test; (4) commit, except at the line.
cards.43.drill: Say the last line in a calm voice, not a challenging one.
cards.43.traps: "I'd refuse". "I'd just do it". A preachy, holier-than-thou tone.
cards.44.who: HM, HRBP. Source: the Hearti Lab design system shared with marketing; the JD mentions working across departments. Scored on: a wide view.
cards.44.why: Two memorable opening lines, a real example (Hearti Lab), and a reason tied to trust.
cards.44.five: Support is research, marketing is the promise, with the Hearti Lab example.
cards.44.evidence: ✅ Hearti Lab design system with marketing. ✅ RegShield work with compliance.
cards.44.image: Pantry: **a call-centre headset** hanging next to **a megaphone**.
cards.44.must: (1) support is research; (2) marketing makes the promise, the product keeps it; (3) Hearti Lab example.
cards.44.traps: Only talking about PM and engineering.
cards.45.who: HM (Head of Product), PM. Scored on: product thinking, not just design.
cards.45.why: It speaks the HM's (Head of Product) language. It gives a concrete example of framing. It uses a modern tool (prototyping in code). And it admits the roadmap isn't yours (so it doesn't threaten the HM).
cards.45.five: A ranked list of user problems + the fulfilment example framed in business language + "roadmap isn't mine".
cards.45.evidence: ✅ Fulfilment 24h → 5 minutes. 🟨 "framing got it prioritised": confirm your part in the prioritising.
cards.45.image: Pantry: **a menu** (the roadmap) on the fridge. You stick **a ranking chart** next to it.

cards.46.who: HM, HRBP, CEO. Source: reviews mention clients and partners in Dubai; the G-local principle. Scored on: international experience, cultural awareness.
cards.46.why: Three concrete pieces of international evidence, a practical tool (async), and a deep cultural insight about Vietnamese teams (a Vietnamese interviewer will nod). It doesn't mention Dubai directly, but it answers the real concern.
cards.46.five: Three pieces of international evidence + async + one insight about Vietnamese team culture.
cards.46.evidence: ✅ LSEG 190 countries. ✅ about 15 years in Singapore. ✅ weekly calls for the freelance work. 🟨 "between Singapore, Australia": confirm the real places you work with at NAB.

cards.46.must: (1) three pieces of evidence; (2) async; (3) understanding Vietnamese team culture.
cards.46.traps: Generalising about a culture in a negative way. Asking about Dubai here (save that for Part 13).
cards.47.who: HM, CEO, HRBP. Source: the "Own" and "Drive" culture; a Lead role with no direct management authority. Scored on: how you influence.
cards.47.why: The story is very close to Qualgo's world (AI + data safety). It has a clear order of influence (proof → safe → easy). It has an honest number labelled as an estimate. And it ends with a real award.
cards.47.five: Proof → safe → easy, quote the Q2 FY26 award word for word, label the 60% as an estimate, and give adoption results with numbers.
cards.47.evidence: ✅ AI adoption lead since March 2026. ✅ Q2 FY26 (We Win Together), citation "uplifting team capability through practical AI guidance". ✅ RegShield about 60% / half the time (estimate). 🟨 **specific adoption results** (how many people, how often).
cards.47.hook: **"Proof · Safe · Easy."** (P-S-E, "Phở Sáng Em", picture a bowl of pho in the morning). 60% · ½ · award.
cards.47.image: Pantry, sink: **a small robot** (AI) is washing 6 of 10 mugs. Above the sink hangs a sign, **"Approved soap only"** (safe). Next to it stands **an award trophy**.
cards.47.must: (1) no authority; (2) start with yourself; (3) data safety; (4) results + award.
cards.47.drill: This story is reused for Q52 (AI in your process). Practise both openings.
cards.47.traps: Saying "measured". Inflating the adoption rate. Telling the award story as if you did it alone: the citation is about *lifting the team's capability*, so put the weight on your colleagues.
cards.48.who: PM, HM, Eng. Source: the "Innovate with purpose" principle; the JD on data-driven work. Scored on: balancing numbers and observation.
cards.48.why: "What vs why" is a classic line, but it goes deeper with "choose the metric first" (a sign of maturity) and an example with both numbers and observation.
cards.48.five: "Choose the metric before" and the SLE example with both observation and numbers.
cards.48.image: Lab: **a microscope** (why) next to **a bar chart** (what).
cards.48.must: (1) both; (2) choose the metric first; (3) SLE example.
cards.48.follow_ups.0.a: **"When a completion rate went up because we removed a step that people actually needed. Completion isn't success. Now I always pair it with a downstream check."** 🟨 (only say it if it really happened; if not, say the principle)
cards.49.who: HM (Head of Product), PM, CEO. Scored on: consumer product thinking, understanding network effects, balancing growth and trust.
cards.49.understand: This question separates designers who think about the product from designers who only do UI. Use Google's **HEART** (Rodden, Hutchinson & Fu, 2010) as the frame, then give a **North Star** and **guardrails**. Special point: explain how to measure under E2EE.
cards.49.why: It has a three-layer structure. The North Star is chosen for a reason (to avoid spam). It uses HEART properly, with concrete metrics for chat and for security. It has guardrails. And it ends with the E2EE constraint, which only someone who understands security would think of.
cards.49.five: A North Star with a reason, HEART with concrete chat and security metrics, guardrails, and "events, not content". Have the HEART table ready for P1.
cards.49.evidence: ✅ Section 9.5. 🟨 direct experience with consumer metrics: limited; say this is the frame you would use.
cards.49.image: Lab: **a North Star** hangs from the ceiling. Below it, **five hearts** (HEART) stand in a row, with **safety railings** (guardrails) around them.
cards.49.must: (1) North Star and why it's not messages sent; (2) HEART with examples; (3) guardrails; (4) E2EE: events, not content.
cards.49.drill: Write out the full HEART table (Goal → Signal → Metric) for the message request feature.
cards.49.traps: Only talking about vanity metrics (downloads, messages sent). Forgetting E2EE. Quoting industry numbers you aren't sure of.
cards.50.who: PM, HM. Source: reviews about the quick pace, a startup inside a large group. Scored on: being practical.
cards.50.why: It starts from the decision (not the method). It has a concrete day-by-day plan. It cites Nielsen's research on 5 users. It understands recruiting in Vietnam. And it uses AI responsibly.
cards.50.five: The 5-day plan + recruiting in Vietnam + "AI drafts, I decide". Use P3 as a real example.
cards.50.image: Lab: **a 5-day calendar**. On days 2 to 4 there are **five chairs** drawn (5 users).
cards.50.must: (1) the decision question; (2) the plan; (3) recruiting in Vietnam; (4) AI, with checking.
cards.50.traps: Proposing a 6-week study. Ignoring data you already have.
cards.51.who: HM, Security/AI Hằng, Eng. Source: Qualgo is hiring for agentic AI and GenAI; the "AI-powered" brand. Scored on: real practice, responsible use, results.
cards.51.understand: This is your clearest strength. Don't just list tools. Talk about the **process**, the **honest numbers**, the **data safety limits** (very important for a security company), and your **role in spreading it** (AI adoption lead).
cards.51.why: The "helps / doesn't / won't" structure shows maturity. The number is labelled as an estimate (honest). The data limits show you fit a security company. And you've spread it to others (the Lead role).
cards.51.five: Helps / doesn't / won't, a clean 2-minute demo with no real data in it, and your role in spreading it.
cards.51.evidence: ✅ RegShield about 60%, about half the time (estimate). ✅ Cursor for the stablecoin wallet. ✅ AI adoption lead since March 2026. ✅ Q2 FY26 We Win Together.
cards.51.image: Lab: the **AI robot** in the corner has **three lights**: green (helps), yellow (doesn't), red (won't). It's **handing out flyers** (spreading it).
cards.51.must: (1) say exactly where AI helps; (2) 60% is an estimate; (3) no data in unapproved tools; (4) the adoption lead role.
cards.51.drill: Prepare a 2-minute demo: one prompt and its result, clean, with no NAB data.
cards.51.follow_ups.0.a: 🟨 only name tools you really use (for example Cursor, Claude, Figma AI).
cards.51.traps: Saying "measured 60%". Listing tools with no process. Hinting that you've put internal data into AI.
cards.52.who: Security/AI Hằng, HM, CEO. Source: "AI-powered secure communication"; hiring for agentic AI. This may be **the central strategy question**. Scored on: understanding the AI/privacy tension, concrete design.
cards.52.understand: The tension: AI needs data; E2EE means the server can't read it. Ways the industry handles this: **on-device processing**, **clear opt-in**, **private computing** (for example, Apple Private Cloud Compute, announced in 2024, is one model to look at). You don't need to explain the tech, only the design principles.
cards.52.why: The opening names the exact tension in one sentence. The four rules are clear and match what the industry does. You link straight to the design pattern you're working on at RegShield. The fourth rule is a product strategy recommendation, which shows you think like a Head of Product.
cards.52.five: Four rules, the RegShield pattern, "protector before assistant", and holding up through two follow-ups on on-device accuracy and agentic AI.
cards.52.evidence: ✅ RegShield: AI suggestion + confidence + correction + audit (MVP, not live). ✅ Design Day Challenge 3 (agentic banking concept). 🟨 technical details of on-device AI: don't make claims about their capabilities.
cards.52.image: Lab: the AI robot **lives inside the phone** (on-device). It has **a small door that only the user's hand can open** (opt-in) and **a screen on its chest that explains things** (explainable). It **holds a shield, not binoculars** (protector, not surveillance).
cards.52.must: (1) the tension; (2) 4 rules; (3) RegShield pattern; (4) protector before assistant.
cards.52.drill: Sketch the "Flagged because…" screen with a button to correct it.
cards.52.traps: Proposing AI that reads every message on the server. Saying "we'll anonymise the data" as if that's enough. Being too technical.
cards.53.who: Security/AI, Eng. Source: Google PAIR's People + AI Guidebook; Microsoft's Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (Amershi et al., 2019). Scored on: designing for probability, not certainty.
cards.53.why: "Design the recovery before the feature" is a line people remember. The three principles are backed by research (Amershi et al. 2019, 18 guidelines). There's a RegShield example. And it shows you understand that, in security, a false positive and a false negative don't cost the same.
cards.53.five: "Recovery before feature", the FP/FN imbalance, and one real AI error you've seen (no internal data).
cards.53.image: Lab: the AI robot **slips on a banana peel**, but there's already **a cushion** under it (recovery).
cards.53.must: (1) recovery first; (2) three principles; (3) RegShield; (4) FP/FN imbalance.
cards.53.drill: Describe one real AI error you saw in RegShield (no internal data). 🟨
cards.53.traps: Saying AI will be right if it's trained well. Showing percentages to everyday users.
